summary:
AHMS (Astronaut Health Monitoring System) is an offline-first health monitoring software we developed for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It collects health data automatically through a simulated bio-harness (heart rate, HRV, SpO2, blood pressure, skin temperature) and cabin sensors (CO2, radiation), plus a short daily check-in and a weekly reaction-time test. Each reading is compared against the astronaut’s own baseline and scored across six domains: cardiovascular, radiation, microgravity, behavioral, environment, and immune.
AHMS addresses the challenge by turning data into action. A three-tier analysis engine flags problems with transparent logic, a Green/Yellow/Orange/Red triage system shows urgency, and symptom checkers, step-by-step protocols, and a medical kit inventory tell the astronaut what to do next. A store-and-forward link handles communication delays and blackouts.
This matters because on Mars missions, help is 20+ minutes away. Astronauts must be able to spot and act on health changes themselves.
details:
Project Details: AHMS (Astronaut Health Monitoring System)

What it does and how it works
AHMS is an offline-first web app that monitors an astronaut’s health during long missions. A simulated bio-harness streams heart rate, HRV, SpO2, blood pressure, and skin temperature at 1 Hz. Cabin sensors add CO2 and radiation readings. The astronaut also completes a short daily check-in (mood, fatigue, sleep, pain) and a weekly 5-trial reaction-time test. Every reading is compared to that astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline, then analyzed in three tiers: simple rules, trends over time, and multi-signal patterns (for example, high CO2 + headache + slow reactions = hypercapnia warning). Results appear as Green/Yellow/Orange/Red status across six domains: cardiovascular, radiation, microgravity, behavioral, environment, and immune. Each alert comes with an action card, a symptom checker, step-by-step protocols, and a medical kit inventory with dose tracking. A store-and-forward link queues messages for the ground team during delays and blackouts.

Benefits

  • Works without Earth contact, so the crew is never waiting on a 20-minute reply.
  • Personal baselines make alerts more accurate for each individual.
  • Plain-language explanations and next-step guidance reduce guesswork under stress.
  • Alert grouping and deduplication limit alert fatigue.
  • Private logs protect sensitive information in a small crew.

Intended impact
To help astronauts catch health problems early and act on them safely and independently on Moon and Mars missions. The same design could also support remote or isolated settings on Earth, such as polar stations.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS
  • Backend: FastAPI with Uvicorn, WebSocket streaming
  • Database: SQLite in WAL mode
  • Frontend: pure HTML5/JS dashboard with a Canvas-based live ECG
  • Testing: Python unittest (7 of 7 tests passing) plus a scenario injector
  • Hardware: none. The sensors are simulated, and real devices would be a future integration.

How it is creative

  • Multi-signal pattern recognition detects syndromes before they become emergencies.
  • The live ECG and glove-friendly, low-light interface are designed for real spaceflight conditions.
  • A delay slider (0 s to 20 min) demonstrates deep-space communication realistically.
  • The system explains its reasoning in plain language, so astronauts can trust it.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay, blackouts, and limited onboard computing and power.
  • Differences between individuals, which is why we use personal baselines.
  • Astronaut workload, so daily input stays under 5 minutes.
  • Privacy and role-based access for astronauts, medical officers, and flight surgeons.
  • Fault tolerance: the system keeps working if a sensor fails and tells the user what is missing.
  • Safety and honesty: this is a prototype validated on simulated data, not flight-certified.
